title: AI Boom or AI Bubble in 2026? A Skeptical Read
body_md:
*Screenshot of sec.gov ([source](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001652044/000165204426000071/goog-20260630.htm))* **My verdict:** There are two different things happening in 2026, and lumping them together is how people get confused. The *usage* of AI tools looks far more durable than the infrastructure financing — ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are widely used products, and AI note-takers and coding assistants are in regular use at many workplaces (this post does not quantify adoption). The *financing* of the infrastructure behind them looks a lot more like a bubble: spending is being funded increasingly by debt and stock sales, on commitments that stretch out years. I'm leading with that split because "is it a bubble?" is usually asked as one question, and answering it as one question gets you the wrong answer for your own situation. If you're a regular person wondering whether to keep paying $20/month for an AI subscription, this is not your problem. If you hold a lot of concentrated tech stock, or your job depends on an AI startup's next funding round, it is. ## What's Actually Going On

*Screenshot of sec.gov ([source](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001652044/000119312526251733/d160205dfwp.htm))* The clearest public evidence isn't in op-eds. It's in company filings, where the numbers are legally binding. Take Alphabet, because its disclosures are unusually specific: 1. On its Q4 2025 earnings call, management guided 2026 capital expenditures to $175–185 billion, after $91 billion of capex in 2025. 2. By the Q1 2026 call, that guidance had moved up. Alphabet's own securities filing says 2026 capex is expected to be $180–$190 billion, and that 2027 capex is expected to increase significantly compared with 2026. 3. Then it moved again. On the Q2 2026 call the CFO raised full-year 2026 guidance to $195–$205 billion, attributing the increase mainly to faster delivery of capacity to meet demand. 4. In the second quarter of 2026 alone, capital expenditures were $44.9 billion, and free cash flow for the quarter was negative $5.9 billion. Read step 4 again. For that quarter, the spending outran the cash the business threw off. The filings don't say any specific raise covers that quarterly gap, but they do show how Alphabet is funding this: in June 2026 it issued stock and mandatory convertible preferred shares for net proceeds of $49.6 billion, for general corporate purposes including capital expenditures to scale AI infrastructure and global compute, plus a $40 billion at-the-market program for Class A and Class C stock expected to begin in Q3 2026. The same documents note $174 billion of operating cash flow over the 12 months ended March 31, 2026, and more than $85 billion of debt raised over the prior year, bringing total debt above $100 billion, and an agreement to sell $10 billion of stock to Berkshire Hathaway in a private placement. The chip-and-model side is structured similarly. OpenAI and NVIDIA announced a partnership to deploy at least 10 gigawatts of AI data centers, with NVIDIA intending to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI progressively as each gigawatt is deployed. So: the chip vendor invests in the customer, who buys chips from the vendor. Nothing in these announcements alleges wrongdoing, but the arrangement is circular, and it's worth naming. ## Where It Breaks

*Screenshot of abc.xyz ([source](https://abc.xyz/investor/events/event-details/2026/2025-Q4-Earnings-Call-2026-Dr_C033hS6/default.aspx))* The bubble case is real, but it's weaker than the loudest version you'll see on social media. Here's where both sides overreach. - **"Huge capex = bubble" skips a step.** Alphabet is funding this partly from $174 billion of operating cash flow over the 12 months ended March 31, 2026. A company printing that much cash spending heavily is different from a 1999 startup with no revenue. - **"People use it, so it's fine" skips a different step.** Your $20 subscription does not pay for a gigawatt. Usage being genuine says nothing about whether *this much* capacity, on *this* schedule, earns its cost of capital. - **Announced capacity isn't delivered capacity.** Gigawatt announcements are press releases; power contracts, land, and transformers are not. NVIDIA's first gigawatt with OpenAI was slated for the second half of 2026 on the Vera Rubin platform; I have no primary source confirming it landed on schedule. Multi-year plans slip. - **Depreciation is the delayed bill.** Depreciation starts when assets are ready for their intended use, and data center projects can run months to years from purchase to service. The spending hits cash now and earnings later. - **Debt changes the failure mode.** Equity-funded overbuilding can be written off without a creditor setting the timing; debt-funded overbuilding can force decisions on a lender's timetable. - **I could not verify the aggregate.** Plenty of outlets publish a combined "Big Five 2026 capex" total in the $600–725 billion range. I found those figures only in secondary summaries and analyst decks, not in a primary disclosure I could stand behind, so I'm not quoting a total. ## One honest caution

*Screenshot of openai.com ([source](https://openai.com/index/openai-nvidia-systems-partnership/))* I'm not a financial adviser and this isn't investment advice. Nothing above tells you whether any stock is overpriced — filings describe spending and funding, not whether that spending pays off. If your retirement savings are concentrated in a handful of AI-exposed names, that's a conversation for someone licensed to have it. *Updated October 2026: this piece is based on SEC filings and official company announcements, not interviews or testing. An earlier version removed unsupported adoption claims, an unsourced annual-discount figure, a legal characterization of the NVIDIA/OpenAI arrangement, and the description of the $49.6 billion raise as earmarked for compute. Sources: [Alphabet 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204426000071/goog-20260630.htm), [Alphabet offering document (FWP)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000119312526251733/d160205dfwp.htm), [Alphabet Q1 2026 earnings call](https://abc.xyz/investor/events/event-details/2026/2026-Q1-Earnings-Call-2026-nW8kCrBAKS/default.aspx), [Claude pricing](https://claude.com/pricing).* ## My Take Three things stood out reading the filings. Guidance moved from $175–185 billion to $180–190 billion to $195–205 billion inside about nine months, which tells me the plans are being rewritten mid-flight rather than executed from a stable budget. I expected capex this size to come out of cash, so a $49.6 billion equity-and-convertible raise plus a $40 billion ATM program reframed the story for me. And the Berkshire placement is a fair point against me: a famously unexcitable long-term investor buying into an AI-infrastructure raise complicates the simplest bubble narrative. My read: this is a capital-structure bubble sitting on top of a real product boom, and those two can unwind separately. The 2027–2028 scenario I'd watch — speculation, not prediction — isn't ChatGPT disappearing. It's a squeeze on the middle layer: GPU-rental companies, thin wrapper startups, tools whose only feature is an API call with a logo on it. The models survive; some of the companies reselling them don't. Concretely: keep the AI tools that save you measurable time, and pay monthly for anything from a vendor you couldn't have named two years ago. Annual prepay is a bet on the vendor still existing, which is a cheap bet with a large company and an expensive one with a startup. Claude Pro, for example, is $200 paid once a year against $240 paid monthly — $40 saved, about 16.7%, for a twelve-month commitment. That's a reasonable trade with Anthropic; I wouldn't make it with a Series A company whose roadmap is the product. I'm not a financial professional, and none of this is advice about what to buy or sell. If the bull case is right, I'll have been too cautious about the middle layer. I'd rather be wrong in that direction than tell you to prepay three years of a startup's roadmap.
